subjective.question: What is accounting? Define financial information and financial position.
subjective.answer: Accounting is a language that is used to communicate and understand the financial ideas, financial expressions, financial thoughts and financial information of a business. Financial information is any information that is measurable in terms of money and causes a change in the financial position of an entity. Financial position means an entity's status of resources and sources. Resources are the assets that an entity holds in its control, and sources are the means of finance through which the entity makes such assets. Sources of finance include liabilities and owner's equity, so: Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity.

subjective.question: What are the three sources of financial information? Explain each briefly.
subjective.answer: There are three sources of financial information, also known as accounting phenomena: 1. Transactions: These are the outcome of dealings made, e.g. purchase of goods, sale of goods, payment of expenses. 2. Events: These are the outcome of incidents that happen. Events are of two types: monetary events and non-monetary events.

subjective.question: Conditions: These are the adjustments in the recorded information, e.g. depreciation of assets, provisions for doubtful debts.
Who are the users of financial information?
subjective.answer: The users of financial information are: 1. Investors / shareholders / owners 2. Trade contacts (customers and suppliers) 3. Lenders

subjective.question: Taxation authorities
Managers and employees
Financial consultants and advisers
Government
General public
Distinguish between sole proprietorship, partnership and joint stock company.
subjective.answer: Sole Proprietorship: A sole proprietorship (sole trader) is a business owned and run by one individual. There is no legal distinction between the owner and the business; all profits and losses belong to the owner, all assets are owned by him and all debts of the business are his personal debts, so his liability is unlimited. Partnership: A partnership is a business in which two or more partners (owners) share the profits or losses of the business with each other. Partners may be exposed to personal liability for the debts of the firm. Joint Stock Company: A joint stock company is a business entity in which certificates of ownership (shares) are issued by the company in return for each financial contribution. The shareholders are free to transfer their ownership by selling their shares to others. It offers the protection of limited liability: a shareholder is not liable for any of the company's debts beyond the face value of his shareholding. Joint stock companies are of two kinds: private and public companies.

subjective.question: Differentiate between capital expenditure and revenue expenditure.
subjective.answer: Capital Expenditure: These are expenses whose benefits last for a longer period, i.e. the benefits are enjoyed by the business in the current period as well as in the years to come. Capital expenditure always results in an increase in assets. For example, when a vehicle is purchased by the business, the amount expended is capital expenditure and the vehicle is shown in the balance sheet as an asset. Revenue Expenditure: These are expenses whose benefits do not last for a longer period and are restricted to the current period only; no more benefits are to be enjoyed by the business in the coming periods. For example, salaries, utility bills and fuel bills paid, against which the organization enjoyed benefits for the current period only. Revenue expenditure is charged to the profit and loss account.

subjective.question: State with reasons whether the following items of expenditure are capital or revenue in nature: (1) Wages paid on the purchase of goods. (2) Carriage paid on goods purchased. (3) Transportation paid on purchase of machinery. (4) Octroi duty paid on machinery. (5) Octroi duty paid on goods. (6) A second-hand car was purchased for Rs. 7,000 and Rs. 5,000 were spent on its repair and overhauling. (7) Office building was whitewashed at a cost of Rs. 3,000. (8) A new machinery was purchased for Rs. 80,000 and Rs. 1,000 was spent on its installation. (9) Old furniture was repaired at a cost of Rs. 500. (10) Land was purchased for Rs. 100,000 and Rs. 5,000 was paid as legal expenses.
subjective.answer: 1. Revenue expenditure — wages on purchase of goods are part of the cost of goods for the current period. 2. Revenue expenditure — carriage inwards is a trading expense of the current period. 3. Capital expenditure — transportation paid to bring the machinery to the business is part of the cost of the asset. 4. Capital expenditure — octroi duty on machinery is paid to acquire the asset, so it is added to its cost. 5. Revenue expenditure — octroi duty on goods is a normal trading expense. 6. Capital expenditure — both the purchase price (Rs. 7,000) and the repair/overhauling charges (Rs. 5,000) are capital, because the repairs were necessary to bring the second-hand car into working condition; total cost of the car is Rs. 12,000.

subjective.question: Revenue expenditure — whitewashing is a maintenance expense of the current period.
Capital expenditure — purchase price (Rs. 80,000) plus installation charges (Rs. 1,000) are both part of the cost of machinery, i.e. Rs. 81,000.
Revenue expenditure — repair of old furniture only maintains the existing asset.
Capital expenditure — legal expenses paid on the purchase of land form part of the cost of land, i.e. Rs. 105,000.
Differentiate between the cash basis and the accrual basis of accounting.
subjective.answer: Cash basis: It is a system in which transactions are recorded only when cash is received or paid. This system reports income when it is received and expenses when they are paid. Accrual basis: It is a system in which transactions are recorded on the basis of the amount becoming due for payment or receipt, regardless of whether settlement in terms of cash has happened or not. Income is recorded when it is earned and expenses are recorded when they are incurred.

subjective.question: How is the double entry bookkeeping system different from the single entry bookkeeping system?
subjective.answer: In the double entry system, every transaction is recorded twice — once on the debit side and once on the credit side — because every transaction has two aspects: receiving and giving. It is a complete system: personal, real and nominal accounts are all maintained, a trial balance can be prepared to check arithmetical accuracy, and complete financial statements (trading and profit & loss account and balance sheet) can be prepared. In the single entry system, only one aspect of a transaction (or sometimes no aspect) is recorded. Generally only personal accounts and a cash book are maintained; real and nominal accounts are ignored. It is an incomplete and unscientific system: no trial balance can be prepared, true profit cannot be ascertained accurately, and the financial position of the business cannot be known reliably.

subjective.question: What is the accounting equation? Explain its components.
subjective.answer: In accounting, the resources controlled by a business are its assets, and the sources of such inputs are owner's equity and liabilities. Therefore: Assets = Owner's Equity + Liabilities The owner's equity itself changes with the results of the business: Owner's Equity = Capital + Profit (Incomes− Expenses) − Drawings The special feature of this equation is that both sides shall always remain equal, because every transaction affects at least two accounts in such a way that the equality is maintained.

subjective.question: What are the rules of debit and credit?
subjective.answer: Debit (Dr.) comes from the Latin word 'Debere' and Credit (Cr.) from 'Credere'. Dr. and Cr. are also termed as the tools of accounting. Accounts are divided into two groups: Debit group: Assets and Expenses. An increase in these accounts is debited and a decrease is credited. Credit group: Owner's Equity, Liabilities and Incomes. An increase in these accounts is credited and a decrease is debited. Conventionally, accounts are also divided into three types: personal accounts, real accounts and nominal accounts.

subjective.question: Show the effect of the following transactions upon the accounting equation: June 1, Mr. Salman started business with cash Rs. 100,000. June 5, Purchased furniture for cash Rs. 4,000. June 6, Purchased goods for cash Rs. 25,000. June 10, Paid transportation on goods purchased Rs. 1,000. June 12, Sold goods for cash Rs. 15,000, costing Rs. 11,000. June 15, Purchased goods on credit for Rs. 15,000. June 19, Sold goods to Rashid on credit for Rs. 8,000, costing Rs. 6,500. June 25, Received cash from Rashid Rs. 4,000. June 28, Cash paid to creditor Rs. 9,000. June 30, Paid rent and salaries for the month Rs. 4,000.
subjective.answer: Effect on the accounting equation (Assets = Liabilities + Capital): June 1: Cash increases Rs. 100,000; Capital increases Rs. 100,000. June 5: Furniture increases Rs. 4,000; Cash decreases Rs. 4,000. (No change in total assets.) June 6: Stock increases Rs. 25,000; Cash decreases Rs. 25,000. June 10: Cash decreases Rs. 1,000; Capital decreases Rs. 1,000 (expense). June 12: Cash increases Rs. 15,000; Stock decreases Rs. 11,000; Capital increases Rs. 4,000 (profit). June 15: Stock increases Rs. 15,000; Creditors (liability) increase Rs. 15,000. June 19: Debtors increase Rs. 8,000; Stock decreases Rs. 6,500; Capital increases Rs. 1,500 (profit). June 25: Cash increases Rs. 4,000; Debtors decrease Rs. 4,000. June 28: Cash decreases Rs. 9,000; Creditors decrease Rs. 9,000. June 30: Cash decreases Rs. 4,000; Capital decreases Rs. 4,000 (expenses). Final position: Assets = Cash Rs. 76,000 + Furniture Rs. 4,000 + Stock Rs. 22,500 + Debtors Rs. 4,000 = Rs. 106,500. Liabilities + Capital = Creditors Rs. 6,000 + Capital Rs. 100,500 = Rs. 106,500. Both sides are equal.

subjective.question: What is a voucher? Explain the types of vouchers.
subjective.answer: A voucher is an internal document that is prepared to witness that a transaction is complete and verified; it is supported by the needful documents and authorized by the appropriate signatories. Types of vouchers: 1. Journal Voucher 2. Cash Payment Voucher 3. Bank Receipt and Payment Voucher 4. Gift Voucher

subjective.question: What is a journal? Write down the advantages of a journal.
subjective.answer: A journal is the book of original (prime) entry in which transactions are recorded in chronological order, showing the accounts to be debited and credited, before they are posted to the ledger. Advantages of journal: 1. It provides a permanent and chronological record of all transactions. 2. It shows, at one place, the complete story of a transaction with its narration. 3. It reduces the chances of errors, because the debit and credit of each transaction are recorded together and can be checked. 4. It helps in locating and rectifying errors. 5. It facilitates the posting of transactions to the ledger accounts. 6. Transactions which cannot be recorded in any other book of prime entry are recorded in the journal.

subjective.question: Briefly explain the features of a trial balance.
subjective.answer: A trial balance is a statement of all the open debit and credit balances in a double-entry ledger, prepared to test their equality. Its features are: 1. It is a statement, not an account; it is prepared on a particular date. 2. It contains the balances of all ledger accounts — personal, real and nominal. 3. It is prepared to check the arithmetical accuracy of the books: if the total of the debit side equals the total of the credit side, the books are assumed to be arithmetically correct. 4. It helps in locating errors, although it does not disclose all types of errors (e.g. errors of omission or principle). 5. It forms the basis for preparing the final accounts (trading and profit & loss account and balance sheet).

subjective.question: Record the following transactions in the General Journal: Jan 1, 2007 — Mr. Asghar started business with cash Rs. 100,000. Jan 2, 2007 — Opened bank account with Rs. 50,000. Jan 4, 2007 — Purchased goods for cash Rs. 15,000. Jan 9, 2007 — Payment made to Karachi Store (creditor) Rs. 15,000 by cheque. Jan 14, 2007 — Goods returned to Karachi Store worth Rs. 1,500. Jan 22, 2007 — Goods sold for cash Rs. 2,000.
subjective.answer: General Journal: Jan 1, 2007: Cash A/c Dr. 100,000 — To Capital A/c 100,000 (Business started with cash) Jan 2, 2007: Bank A/c Dr. 50,000 — To Cash A/c 50,000 (Bank account opened) Jan 4, 2007: Purchases A/c Dr. 15,000 — To Cash A/c 15,000 (Goods purchased for cash) Jan 9, 2007: Karachi Store A/c Dr. 15,000 — To Bank A/c 15,000 (Payment made to creditor by cheque) Jan 14, 2007: Karachi Store A/c Dr. 1,500 — To Purchases Return A/c 1,500 (Goods returned to Karachi Store) Jan 22, 2007: Cash A/c Dr. 2,000 — To Sales A/c 2,000 (Goods sold for cash)

subjective.question: ABC Company purchased goods of Rs. 150,000 on credit, from which goods of Rs. 20,000 were defective and returned. The company received 2% discount at the time of payment from the supplier. What will be the amount of discount received by the company? Also show the journal entries.
subjective.answer: (A) Discount Received = (150,000 − 20,000) × 2/100 = Rs. 2,600 (B) Journal entries: Entry for purchase: Goods (Purchases) A/c Dr. 150,000 — To Accounts Payable A/c 150,000 Entry for return: Accounts Payable A/c Dr. 20,000 — To Goods (Purchases Return) A/c 20,000 Entry at the time of payment: Accounts Payable A/c Dr. 130,000 — To Discount Income A/c 2,600 — To Cash A/c 127,400

subjective.question: Pass the rectifying entries to correct the following errors: (1) Mr. Ali purchased goods of Rs. 1,500 for cash, but the purchase was omitted to be entered in the books. (2) An amount of Rs. 5,000 received from Mr. Amir was credited to the account of Mr. Ameer. (3) Goods returned worth Rs. 500 to Mr. B were wrongly debited to the Sales Account. (4) A purchase of goods from Mr. B of Rs. 400 has been wrongly debited to the Furniture Account. (5) Furniture purchased for cash Rs. 8,000 was posted as purchases.
subjective.answer: Rectification entries: 1. Purchases A/c Dr. 1,500 — To Cash A/c 1,500 (Cash purchase omitted earlier, now recorded) 2. Mr. Ameer A/c Dr. 5,000 — To Mr. Amir A/c 5,000 (Amount received from Mr. Amir wrongly credited to Mr. Ameer, now rectified) 3. Mr. B A/c Dr. 500 — To Sales A/c 500 (Goods returned to Mr. B wrongly debited to Sales A/c, now rectified) 4. Purchases A/c Dr. 400 — To Furniture A/c 400 (Goods purchased from Mr. B wrongly debited to Furniture A/c, now rectified) 5. Furniture A/c Dr. 8,000 — To Purchases A/c 8,000 (Furniture purchased for cash wrongly posted as purchases, now rectified)

subjective.question: Calculate the rate of depreciation of an asset with the help of the given data: Cost of the asset Rs. 120,000; Residual value Rs. 40,000; Expected life 5 years.
subjective.answer: Depreciable amount = Cost − Residual value = 120,000 − 40,000 = Rs. 80,000 Annual depreciation (straight line) = 80,000 / 5 = Rs. 16,000 Rate of depreciation = 16,000 / 80,000 × 100 = 20%

subjective.question: Calculate depreciation of the asset for five years by using the written down value method. Also show accumulated depreciation. Cost of the asset Rs. 120,000; Depreciation rate 10%; Expected life 5 years.
subjective.answer: Written down value method: Year 1: Depreciation = 10% × 120,000 = Rs. 12,000; Accumulated depreciation = Rs. 12,000; Written down value = 120,000 − 12,000 = Rs. 108,000 Year 2: Depreciation = 10% × 108,000 = Rs. 10,800; Accumulated depreciation = Rs. 22,800; Written down value = Rs. 97,200 Year 3: Depreciation = 10% × 97,200 = Rs. 9,720; Accumulated depreciation = Rs. 32,520; Written down value = Rs. 87,480 Year 4: Depreciation = 10% × 87,480 = Rs. 8,748; Accumulated depreciation = Rs. 41,268; Written down value = Rs. 78,732 Year 5: Depreciation = 10% × 78,732 = Rs. 7,873.20; Accumulated depreciation = Rs. 49,141.20; Written down value = Rs. 70,858.80

subjective.question: Original cost of a fixed asset is Rs. 500,000, accumulated depreciation is Rs. 166,667 and the revalued amount of the fixed asset is Rs. 600,000. Calculate the written down value and the surplus on revaluation of the fixed asset.
subjective.answer: Written down value = Original cost− Accumulated depreciation = 500,000 − 166,667 = Rs. 333,333 Surplus on revaluation = Revalued amount − Written down value = 600,000 − 333,333 = Rs. 266,667

subjective.question: How is stock valuation made under the FIFO and LIFO methods?
subjective.answer: FIFO (First In, First Out): Under FIFO it is assumed that the stock purchased first is used out first, so the closing stock consists of the stock purchased last, and its value is shown approximately at the latest (last) purchase prices. LIFO (Last In, First Out): Under LIFO it is assumed that the stock purchased last is used first, so the items present in the closing stock are the old ones and are valued at the older prices. LIFO is not used in industry now, and accounting standards prohibit its use.

subjective.question: The following are some of the causes of difference between the Cash Book and the Pass Book balances. If you start with the Cash Book (Dr.) balance in a Bank Reconciliation Statement, will you add them or deduct? (1) Cheques issued but not yet paid by bank. (2) Cheques deposited but not credited by bank. (3) Amount directly deposited into bank by a customer but not recorded in the Cash Book. (4) Dividend collected by bank but not entered in the Cash Book. (5) Insurance premium paid by bank but not recorded in the Cash Book. (6) Cheque deposited but no entry was made in the Cash Book. (7) Bank charges debited by bank but not recorded in the Cash Book. (8) Interest on overdraft debited by bank but not recorded in the Cash Book. (9) Cheque issued but wrongly debited in the Cash Book. (10) Interest credited by bank but not recorded in the Cash Book.
subjective.answer: Starting with the Cash Book (Dr.) balance: 1. Cheques issued but not yet paid by bank — Add 2. Cheques deposited but not credited by bank — Less (deduct) 3. Amount directly deposited by a customer, not recorded in Cash Book — Add 4. Dividend collected by bank, not entered in Cash Book — Add 5. Insurance premium paid by bank, not recorded in Cash Book — Less 6. Cheque deposited but no entry made in Cash Book — Add 7. Bank charges debited by bank, not recorded in Cash Book — Less 8. Interest on overdraft debited by bank, not recorded in Cash Book — Less 9. Cheque issued but wrongly debited in Cash Book — Less 10. Interest credited by bank, not recorded in Cash Book — Add

subjective.question: The following discrepancies were noted on comparing the Cash Book with the Pass Book: Balance as per Cash Book (Cr.) is Rs. 19,000. A cheque for Rs. 5,000 was paid into the bank for collection on 20th March, 2008 but has not yet been collected. Cheques for Rs. 15,000 were issued on 24th March, 2008, out of which cheques for Rs. 10,000 were presented during March, 2008. An amount of Rs. 1,000 for interest on overdraft was debited in the Pass Book but was intimated to Mr. David on 4th April, 2008. Mr. David paid into his bank account an amount of Rs. 3,000 but it was wrongly credited to Mr. Denial's account. On 20th March, 2008 the bank received dividend of Rs. 10,000 from a company in which Mr. David has invested his money; the same had been recorded in the Cash Book on 31st March, 2008. A cheque of Rs. 2,500 was shown in the Pass Book as dishonoured. Prepare a Bank Reconciliation Statement as on 31st March, 2008.
subjective.answer: Bank Reconciliation Statement as on 31st March, 2008: Balance as per Cash Book (Cr. / overdraft) — Rs. 19,000 Add: Cheque deposited but not yet collected — Rs. 5,000 Add: Interest on overdraft debited in the Pass Book only — Rs. 1,000 Add: Amount paid in by Mr. David wrongly credited to Mr. Denial's account — Rs. 3,000 Add: Cheque dishonoured, recorded in the Pass Book only — Rs. 2,500 Less: Unpresented cheques (Rs. 15,000 issued − Rs. 10,000 presented) — Rs. 5,000 Balance as per Pass Book (Cr. / overdraft) — Rs. 25,500 Note: The dividend of Rs. 10,000 appears in both the Cash Book and the Pass Book, so it causes no difference.

subjective.topic: Debtors, Creditors, Bad Debts & Control Accounts
subjective.question: What is the purpose of control accounts?
subjective.answer: A business needs to maintain accounts of individual creditors and debtors in its general ledger. Creditors are the people/entities to whom the company owes money, and debtors are the entities/people who owe money to the business. As a business grows, the number of creditors and debtors also grows, and checking each and every transaction in the general ledger to locate an error becomes very time consuming. Therefore, control accounts are maintained in the general ledger — one for total debtors (debtors control account) and one for total creditors (creditors control account). Individual transactions are recorded in subsidiary ledgers (e.g. sales ledger, purchases ledger) for each debtor and creditor, and periodically the summarized totals are posted to the control accounts. Control accounts help in locating errors quickly, checking the arithmetical accuracy of the subsidiary ledgers, and preparing final accounts without delay.

subjective.topic: Debtors, Creditors, Bad Debts & Control Accounts
subjective.question: State clearly how you will deal with the Bad Debts Account, Provision for Bad Debts Account, Profit & Loss Account and Balance Sheet in the following case: The items appearing in the trial balance are bad debts Rs. 300, provision for bad debts Rs. 350 and sundry debtors Rs. 12,000. It is required to increase the provision for bad debts to 5% on sundry debtors.
subjective.answer: New provision required = 5% × 12,000 = Rs. 600 Treatment in Profit & Loss Account: The P&L Account will be charged with the bad debts of Rs. 300 plus the increase in provision (600− 350 = Rs. 250), i.e. a total charge of Rs. 550. The Bad Debts Account is closed by transferring its balance to the Profit & Loss Account (or against the provision). Treatment in Balance Sheet: On the assets side, Sundry Debtors will be shown after deducting the new provision: Rs. 12,000 − Rs. 600 = Rs. 11,400. The Provision for Bad Debts Account will carry a credit balance of Rs. 600 to the next period.

subjective.topic: Debtors, Creditors, Bad Debts & Control Accounts
subjective.question: On 01-01-2007, the provision for doubtful debts account stood at Rs. 12,000 (credit balance). In 2007, the bad debts amounted to Rs. 10,000. The debtors on 31-12-2007 amounted to Rs. 320,000 and a provision for doubtful debts is to be maintained @ 5%. Show the journal entries and also show how the items will appear in the Profit and Loss Account and the Balance Sheet.
subjective.answer: Journal entries: 1. Bad Debts A/c Dr. 10,000 — To Sundry Debtors A/c 10,000 (Bad debts written off) 2. Provision for Doubtful Debts A/c Dr. 10,000 — To Bad Debts A/c 10,000 (Bad debts transferred to provision account) 3. Profit & Loss A/c Dr. 14,000 — To Provision for Doubtful Debts A/c 14,000 (Provision increased to the required level) Working: Required provision = 5% × 320,000 = Rs. 16,000. Balance of provision after writing off bad debts = 12,000 − 10,000 = Rs. 2,000. Further amount charged to P&L = 16,000 − 2,000 = Rs. 14,000. Profit & Loss Account (extract): To Provision for Doubtful Debts — Rs. 14,000 Balance Sheet (extract), assets side: Sundry Debtors Rs. 320,000 − Less: Provision for Doubtful Debts Rs. 16,000 = Rs. 304,000

subjective.question: Briefly explain the financial statements prepared by an organization. Why are these important for a manufacturing concern?
subjective.answer: The financial statements prepared by any organization are as follows: 1. Profit and Loss Account: It shows the performance of the business in a given period. It shows the profitability of the business, which indicates the success or failure of the business. 2. Balance Sheet: It shows the position of the business at a given point in time. It shows the resources available to the business and the resources invested by the owner and through loans. 3. Cash Flow Statement: It shows the generation of cash and its usage over a given period. Importance for a manufacturing concern: These financial statements are important for a manufacturing concern as they provide information related to the financial affairs of the organization — its profitability and liquidity, the resources available to the company, and the generation of cash and its usage over a given period — which provides reasonable information to the management for taking decisions.

subjective.question: What is the effect of the following adjustments on the Trading & Profit and Loss Account and the Balance Sheet: (1) Outstanding expenses, (2) Prepaid expenses, (3) Accrued income, (4) Income received in advance, (5) Depreciation of assets?
subjective.answer: 1. Outstanding expenses: Added to the relevant expense in the Profit & Loss Account; shown as a current liability in the Balance Sheet. 2. Prepaid expenses: Deducted from the relevant expense in the Profit & Loss Account (only the actual expense of the period is charged); shown as a current asset in the Balance Sheet. 3. Accrued income: Added to the relevant income in the Profit & Loss Account; shown as a current asset in the Balance Sheet. 4. Income received in advance: Deducted from the relevant income in the Profit & Loss Account; shown as a current liability in the Balance Sheet. 5. Depreciation of assets: Charged as an expense in the Profit & Loss Account; deducted from the value of the relevant asset in the Balance Sheet.

subjective.question: With the help of the given data, prepare the Capital Account of a sole trader and calculate the closing balance of capital: Balance b/f Rs. 550,000; Drawings Rs. 50,000; Profit & Loss Account (debit balance) Rs. 45,000.
subjective.answer: Capital Account: Debit side: To Profit & Loss A/c (loss) — Rs. 45,000; To Drawings A/c — Rs. 50,000; To Balance c/f — Rs. 455,000. Total — Rs. 550,000 Credit side: By Balance b/f — Rs. 550,000. Total — Rs. 550,000 Closing balance of capital = 550,000 − 45,000 − 50,000 = Rs. 455,000

subjective.topic: Stock, Cost of Goods Sold & Manufacturing Accounts
subjective.question: What is a manufacturing account? What are its main components?
subjective.answer: A manufacturing account is prepared by a manufacturing concern to calculate the cost of goods manufactured (factory cost) during a period. It is prepared before the trading account, and the factory cost is transferred to the trading account. Main components: 1. Direct materials consumed = Opening stock of raw material + Purchases of raw material + Carriage inwards − Closing stock of raw material. 2. Direct labour (wages paid to workers directly engaged in production). 3. Direct expenses (e.g. royalty on production). Prime Cost = Direct materials consumed + Direct labour + Direct expenses. 4. Factory overheads (indirect factory costs: factory rent, factory salaries, depreciation of plant, power and fuel, etc.). Factory Cost (cost of goods manufactured) = Prime Cost + Factory Overheads + Opening work in process − Closing work in process.

subjective.topic: Stock, Cost of Goods Sold & Manufacturing Accounts
subjective.question: What is cost of goods sold? How is it calculated for a trading concern and for a manufacturing concern?
subjective.answer: Cost of goods sold is the cost of the goods that have been sold during a period. For a trading concern: Cost of goods sold = Opening stock + Purchases + Carriage inwards (direct expenses) − Closing stock. Purchases are taken net of purchases returns, and goods withdrawn by the owner or distributed as free samples are also deducted. For a manufacturing concern: Cost of goods sold = Opening stock of finished goods + Cost of goods manufactured (factory cost, taken from the manufacturing account) − Closing stock of finished goods.

subjective.question: Write down the five advantages of a limited company.
subjective.answer: 1. It is a legal entity created by law, and hence has its own recognition, goodwill and brand equity. 2. It is a wide form of business, and hence a formal approach for various partners/investors to come and work for the same objectives in an organized form. 3. Liability of the members is limited to the company assets only; investors/partners are not personally liable for any loss or in the state of bankruptcy. 4. Being a legal entity, it is easy to get loans or gather funds from the public (for public limited companies) or from financial institutions. 5. Being a legal entity, it can enjoy more opportunities for mega projects and trade/operations opportunities in international markets on its own behalf.

subjective.question: What is the difference between a public limited company and a private limited company?
subjective.answer: Private Limited Company: The number of members in a private limited company varies from 2 to 50. It cannot offer its shares to the general public, and its shares are usually held by a small group of people. A minimum of two members form its board of directors, which is given the responsibility to run the day-to-day business of the company. Public Limited Company: In a public limited company there is no restriction on the maximum number of members; a minimum of seven members are required to form it. A public limited company can offer its shares to the general public and its shares are freely transferable.

subjective.question: Write a note on the legal documents required for the formation of a company.
subjective.answer: When someone wants to form a company in Pakistan, he contacts the SECP (Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan), which regulates the affairs of limited companies under the Companies Ordinance 1984. The main legal documents required for the formation of a company are: 1. Memorandum of Association: It is the charter of the company which defines the limitations and powers of the company — its name, registered office, objectives, liability of members and share capital. For a private limited company, at least 2 members subscribe their names to the memorandum, while for a public limited company 7 members subscribe. 2. Articles of Association: It contains the rules and regulations for the internal management of the company and defines the relation of the company with its members. These documents, along with the other requirements of the Companies Ordinance, are filed with the SECP for the registration (incorporation) of the company, after which the company comes into existence as a separate legal entity.

subjective.question: Write down the distinguishing features of a limited company which differentiate it from a sole proprietorship.
subjective.answer: 1. Separate legal entity: A company has a legal existence separate from its members; a sole proprietorship has no existence separate from its owner. 2. Limited liability: The liability of the shareholders of a company is limited to the amount of share capital contributed by them, and their personal wealth is not at stake. A sole proprietor has unlimited liability and must pay the business liabilities from his own wealth. 3. Capital: A company mobilizes the resources of a large number of people, so the problem of extra capital is reduced to the minimum; a sole proprietor depends only on his own resources. 4. Management: A company is managed by experts (board of directors); a sole proprietorship is managed by the owner himself. 5. Perpetual succession: The life of a company is not affected by the death or insolvency of a member; a sole proprietorship comes to an end with the death or insolvency of the proprietor. 6. Transferability: Shares of a company can be transferred freely; ownership of a sole proprietorship cannot be transferred in parts. 7. Legal control: In Pakistan, the affairs of limited companies are controlled by the Companies Ordinance 1984 and governed by the SECP; a sole proprietorship has no such legal formalities. A company also enjoys certain tax benefits which a sole proprietor cannot enjoy.

subjective.question: If the capitals of the partners are fixed, pass journal entries for the following: (1) Drawings made by a partner, (2) Excess drawn amount returned by a partner, (3) Profit distribution among partners.
subjective.answer: When capitals are fixed, all adjustments are made through the partners' current accounts: 1. Drawings made by partner: Partner's Current A/c Dr. — To Cash/Bank A/c 2. Excess drawn amount returned by partner: Cash/Bank A/c Dr. — To Partner's Current A/c 3. Profit distribution among partners: Profit & Loss A/c Dr. — To Partners' Current A/c

subjective.question: Mr. Hassan is a partner in a partnership firm. His capital on July 1, 2001 was Rs. 400,000. He invested further capital of Rs. 150,000 on March 01, 2002. Markup rate is 6% p.a. The financial year of the business is from 1st July to 30th June. Calculate his markup on capital at the end of 30th June 2002.
subjective.answer: (a) Capital invested on July 1, 2001 = Rs. 400,000 (for the full year of 12 months) Markup = 6% × 400,000 = Rs. 24,000 (b) Further capital introduced on March 1, 2002 = Rs. 150,000 (for 4 months, from March 1 to June 30, 2002) Markup = 6% × 150,000 × 4/12 = Rs. 3,000 Total markup on capital = 24,000 + 3,000 = Rs. 27,000

subjective.question: The financial year decided by the partnership agreement is 1st July to 30th June. Mr. Ali is a partner having a capital of Rs. 1,500,000 on July 1, 2007. He introduced more capital of Rs. 10,000 on August 1, 2007, Rs. 500,000 on April 1, 2008 and Rs. 5,000 on June 1, 2008. Markup rate is 10% p.a. Calculate the markup on Mr. Ali's capital for the year ending 30th June 2008.
subjective.answer: Markup is calculated for the period each amount remained invested: Capital of Rs. 1,500,000 for 12 months: 1,500,000 × 10% = Rs. 150,000 Capital of Rs. 10,000 for 11 months (Aug 1, 2007 to Jun 30, 2008): 10,000 × 10% × 11/12 = Rs. 917 Capital of Rs. 500,000 for 3 months (Apr 1 to Jun 30, 2008): 500,000 × 10% × 3/12 = Rs. 12,500 Capital of Rs. 5,000 for 1 month (Jun 1 to Jun 30, 2008): 5,000 × 10% × 1/12 = Rs. 42 Total markup on capital = 150,000 + 917 + 12,500 + 42 = Rs. 163,459 (approximately)

subjective.question: X and Y were partners in a business sharing profits in the ratio of 3:1. Their capitals were Rs. 30,000 and Rs. 10,000 respectively. They earned a net profit of Rs. 160,000. Mr. Y was entitled to a salary of Rs. 200 per month. Prepare the Profit Distribution Account of X & Y partnership.
subjective.answer: Profit Distribution Account: Net profit for the year — Rs. 160,000 Less: Salary of Mr. Y (Rs. 200 × 12 months) — Rs. 2,400 Distributable profit — Rs. 157,600 Share of X (3/4 × 157,600) — Rs. 118,200 Share of Y (1/4 × 157,600) — Rs. 39,400 In addition, Y is credited with his salary of Rs. 2,400, so the total amount credited to Y is Rs. 41,800.

subjective.question: What is a partnership deed? What are its main contents?
subjective.answer: A partnership deed is the written agreement between the partners which contains the terms and conditions of the partnership. It is prepared at the time of the formation of the partnership firm to avoid future disputes. Main contents of a partnership deed: 1. Name and address of the firm and of the partners. 2. Nature of the business. 3. Capital contributed by each partner. 4. Profit and loss sharing ratio. 5. Rate of interest/markup on capital and on drawings, if any. 6. Salary or commission payable to any partner, if any. 7. Duties, powers and obligations of the partners. 8. Rules for the settlement of accounts on the retirement, death or dissolution of the firm.
